blocks.text: Using 2.8 cm wavelength microwave equipment (Fig.15.6), we can observe an interference pattern. The microwave transmitter is directed towards the double gap in a metal barrier. The microwaves are diffracted at the two gaps so that they spread out into the region beyond, where they can be detected using the probe receiver. By moving the probe around, it is possible to detect regions of high intensity (constructive interference) and low intensity (destructive interference). The probe may be connected to a meter, or to an audio amplifier and loudspeaker to give an audible output.

blocks.alt: A bench seen from above. On the left a microwave transmitter points at a row of metal sheets that leave two narrow gaps. Beyond the gaps on the right is a microwave probe, wired to a meter.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.6: Microwaves can also be used to show interference effects (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.6).
